gaplens.pageTitle: GapLens — find, fill and compare gaps in hydroclimate records · Mahfujur Rahman Joy
gaplens.problem: Find, fill and compare gaps in hydroclimate records. Load a streamflow, water-level, rainfall or groundwater record with its neighbours and GapLens maps the gaps, recommends methods, ranks 70+ filling methods by hiding real observations and scoring how well each one restores them, and fills the record.
method: Diagnose: which kinds of gap the record contains, and what they may mean for the choice of method.

Suggest: methods ranked for the gap types found. The score adds the usual choice for this kind of variable, how well the method suits the gap types found, gap length, available neighbours and special rules. This is advice before testing.

Compare: observed values are hidden in blocks of several lengths (or in blocks like your real gaps), every method fills them, and the result is scored against what was hidden. Real gaps are never scored.
Fill: methods are applied in order: the first fills every gap it can, the next fills what is left. Observed values are never changed. Every filled value is flagged in the file you download.

Validate two series: for an observation and a simulation (model output, a product, a second gauge, a rating curve). The tool aligns them, looks for a time lag, a unit factor or a datum offset, then reports metrics with block-bootstrap intervals and qualitative ratings, and tests which correction helps under cross-validation.
Calibrate: fit the parameters of a power-law rating curve, a linear reservoir or GR4J to an observed series, with split-sample or cross-validation.
Rating curve: fit a stage-discharge curve to gaugings, adjust it by hand against the gaugings, and use it to fill or convert a record. Includes automatic segments and year-by-year curves.
Runs in your browser with Python (Pyodide): the page's /api/ requests are answered by the real gaplens Python package, running in a Web Worker with Pyodide, instead of a server.
gaplens.data: One date column, then one column per series: the series to fill, neighbouring stations, drivers. A missing value can be empty, NaN or a code such as -999; the diagnosis finds such codes. Excel files and hydrometric downloads (for example BWDB) also work: title rows, HIGH / LOW rows, a separate time column and serial-number columns are handled, and irregular readings within a day become daily means. Built-in examples: synthetic records with known true values, so a fill can be checked against the truth.
limitations: Whether gaps are random (MCAR), depend on other observed values (MAR) or on the missing value itself (MNAR) cannot be proven from the data. The tool reports what the tests allow and flags a suspicion of MNAR when gaps sit next to extremes.
Methods ranked for the gap types found: this is advice before testing.
The first visit downloads about 40 MB (Python, numpy, pandas, scipy, scikit-learn, statsmodels). Later visits load from the browser cache.
The page needs an internet connection on the first visit to load Python from cdn.jsdelivr.net.
Every example is synthetic.

hydro-series.pageTitle: Hydro-Series Toolkit — Min-Max-Avg & Series Generator · Mahfujur Rahman Joy
hydro-series.problem: Min-Max-Avg Terminal — daily, monthly and yearly minimum, maximum and average from any date + value series (water level, discharge, rainfall…). Export to Excel. Series Generator — fills missing values and extends a record by years, learning its seasonality, spread and day-to-day memory. Includes an accuracy test.
method: The generator learns the seasonal pattern, the spread, the shape of the distribution and the day-to-day memory of your series, then fills the holes inside it or adds years before or after it.

Fill missing values: fills the holes inside the record. The best estimate follows the seasonal pattern and the day-to-day memory of your series, anchored to the values on both sides of each hole. Real data is never changed. Methods: Best estimate (model); Realistic (random, keeps variability); Straight line between neighbours; Seasonal average.
Accuracy test: hides parts of your real record that are known, fills them again with the model and compares with the truth. Shows how far to trust the filled values for holes of that length.
Extend the series: creates new years that behave like your record: the same seasonal pattern, spread, distribution and day-to-day memory. It continues from the last (or first) real value.

Statistical model builds new values from what it learned about your series (seasonal level and spread, distribution, day-to-day memory). Repeat real years copies whole real years, chosen at random for each new year: exact real values, but nothing new can appear.

Transform: how values are treated before learning. Auto uses a log scale for flow-like data (never negative, long upper tail, as in discharge) and no transform for levels. Generated flows never go below zero.
Random seed: a number that fixes the random draw. Same seed and same settings give the same result every time.
hydro-series.data: An .xlsx, .csv or .txt file with one date column and one value column. Dates such as 2024-01-31 06:00 or 31-JAN-2024 06:00:00 AM both work. The columns are found automatically. For the generator: river discharge or water level, daily or monthly, 5 years or more is best; a workbook with several sheets can be processed in one go. 'Try an example' loads a built-in series marked 'EXAMPLE · SYNTHETIC DATA'.
limitations: These are plausible synthetic years, not forecasts.
Repeat real years copies whole real years, chosen at random for each new year: exact real values, but nothing new can appear.
River discharge or water level, daily or monthly, 5 years or more is best.

openffa.pageTitle: OpenFFA — flood frequency analysis · Mahfujur Rahman Joy
openffa.problem: OpenFFA is a flood frequency analysis (FFA) tool that runs entirely in a web browser, with no server, no installation and no data upload. It is meant for water-resources engineers and researchers, with Bangladesh-style records (BWDB discharge and water-level series, April–March water years) as the main context, and it works for any annual-maximum or daily record.
method: Checks before fitting: record length and gaps; Mann-Kendall trend with the Hamed-Rao correction, plus the Theil-Sen slope; Pettitt change point; lag-1 autocorrelation and the Wald-Wolfowitz test; Mann-Whitney homogeneity; Grubbs-Beck (B17B) and Multiple Grubbs-Beck (B17C) outlier tests.
11 distributions: Normal, LN2, LN3, Gumbel, GEV, Pearson III, log-Pearson III, Gamma, Weibull, GLO, GPA.

6 estimation methods: L-moments, maximum likelihood (including censored/historic data), method of moments (B17B), PWM, the Expected Moments Algorithm of Bulletin 17C, and Gumbel's finite-sample method.
Model comparison: KS, AD, CvM and PPCC statistics with bootstrap-calibrated p-values (not tables); AIC, AICc and BIC; L-moment ratio diagram; a transparent ranking with caveats.

Design floods: any return periods; parametric/non-parametric bootstrap (percentile, BC or BCa limits), delta-method and profile-likelihood intervals; probability paper (Gumbel, normal, log-T, Weibull axes).

Further analyses: peaks over threshold (declustering, mean residual life and parameter-stability plots, GPA, intervals that include the event-rate uncertainty) and a non-stationary GEV (trend in location/scale with a likelihood-ratio test).
Heavy calculations run in a Web Worker with progress and Cancel. Bootstrap results are reproducible from a seed.
references: England, J.F., Jr., Cohn, T.A., Faber, B.A., Stedinger, J.R., Thomas, W.O., Jr., Veilleux, A.G., Kiang, J.E., Mason, R.R., Jr. (2018, v1.1 2019). Stedinger, J.R., Vogel, R.M., Foufoula-Georgiou, E. (1993). Frequency analysis of extreme events. In: Maidment, D.R. (ed.), Handbook of Hydrology, ch. 18. McGraw-Hill.
Gumbel, E.J. (1958). Statistics of Extremes. Columbia University Press, New York.
Hamed, K.H., Rao, A.R. (1998). A modified Mann-Kendall trend test for autocorrelated data. Journal of Hydrology, 204, 182–196.
Pettitt, A.N. (1979). A non-parametric approach to the change-point problem. Applied Statistics, 28(2), 126–135.
Efron, B. (1987). Better bootstrap confidence intervals. Journal of the American Statistical Association 82(397), 171–185.
openffa.data: Paste, CSV/TXT or Excel upload, with delimiter, header and date-format detection. Supports annual maxima or daily/sub-daily series with water-year extraction and completeness checks, historic floods (perception threshold), zero flows, low outliers and manual thresholds. The sample data are public domain (USGS) or come from Coles (2001) via R ismev, cited in each file. No Bangladeshi dataset is bundled; the monsoon sample is synthetic.
validation: Every estimator is compared automatically with independent implementations and published results.
R: lmom 3.3 (Hosking), extRemes 2.2.1, ismev 1.43, MGBT 1.1.8 (USGS), trend 1.1.10. Python: SciPy 1.18, lmoments3, pymannkendall, pyhomogeneity.

Bulletin 17C, Appendix 10 (PeakFQ results): Moose River (systematic record, weighted skew); Orestimba Creek (12 zeros, 30 low outliers); Santa Cruz River (22-year historic period plus 10 low outliers). EMA moments are reproduced to the printed 4 decimals and quantiles to the printed 4 significant figures.
Coles (2001): Port Pirie (GEV ML, standard errors, normal and profile-likelihood intervals) and Fremantle (GEV with a linear trend).
Generated by npm run validate on 2026-11-03. Total: 2558 numerical comparisons in 205 groups.
Reference values were produced by running these packages, never typed from memory.
limitations: Methods not implemented: Kappa and Wakeby distributions; LH-moments; mixed-population (e.g. snowmelt + rain) models; regional frequency analysis (index flood, regional L-moment algorithm, discordancy and heterogeneity measures); Bayesian estimation (as in FLIKE / RMC-BestFit) and expected-probability adjustments.

Bulletin 17C analytical EMA confidence intervals (Cohn et al. 2001) and the EMA skew MSE are not implemented. OpenFFA's EMA intervals are a parametric bootstrap that re-simulates the same censoring/historic design. Do not present them as the B17C interval.
The non-stationary GEV allows linear trends in location and log-scale only, with a constant shape. There is no non-stationary GPA or LP3.

Bootstrap interval coverage: in OpenFFA's simulations (n = 30, 90 % nominal, 100-year flood) the parametric bootstrap covered 86–87 %, the non-parametric percentile bootstrap 74–79 % and the non-parametric BCa 77–85 %. All under-cover somewhat; treat intervals as a lower bound on uncertainty.
GOF tests have little power for typical record lengths (20–60 years). A large p-value is not evidence that a distribution is correct.
Confidence intervals describe sampling uncertainty under the chosen model. They exclude model choice, rating-curve and measurement errors, and non-stationarity.

The MGBT decision can be sensitive near the significance cut-off. In Bulletin 17C Example 2 (Orestimba Creek), the USGS MGBT R package and OpenFFA find 38 PILFs where PeakFQ 7.1 found 30. Use judgement and the manual threshold.
No Bangladeshi dataset is bundled; the monsoon sample is synthetic.

brishti-idf.pageTitle: Brishti IDF — rainfall intensity–duration–frequency analysis · Mahfujur Rahman Joy
brishti-idf.problem: Rainfall intensity–duration–frequency (IDF) analysis that runs entirely in your web browser. Nothing is uploaded: the data never leave your computer. The tool was built with Bangladesh's data situation in mind (many daily gauges, few sub-daily ones), but works anywhere.
method: Quality control: gaps, negative and implausible values, flat-lined sensors, long dry runs in wet months, record length, Mann–Kendall trend test, and a record-strip chart.

Annual maxima: sliding (rolling) windows for any durations (default 5 min to 48 h), calendar or water year, coverage rules, a fixed-interval (Hershfield) correction, and the empirical correction factor when sub-daily data exist.

Frequency analysis: Gumbel, GEV, Log-Pearson III, Log-Normal (2- and 3-parameter), Gamma, Pearson III and GLO, fitted by L-moments, moments or maximum likelihood (GEV also by L-moments with a fixed shape, and by penalised likelihood, experimental). Candidates ranked by AICc, BIC, Anderson–Darling, probability-plot correlation or KS; bootstrap confidence intervals; parametric-bootstrap p-values.

Peaks over threshold: independent storms above a threshold, generalised Pareto or exponential excesses (L-moments or ML), Poisson conversion to annual return periods, a threshold-stability table, and the option to use the result for design.

IDF equations: the Koutsoyiannis et al. (1998) general IDF (Gumbel/GEV; robust, one-step least-squares and likelihood estimation), plus Talbot, Bernard, Sherman, Kimijima, a general four-parameter form and three unified-in-T forms. Fitting uses multi-start and differential-evolution optimisation.

Short durations from daily data: IMD formula, calibrated power law, simple scaling, depth-ratio transfer from a nearby sub-daily station, your own ratio table, and Bell (experimental), shown side by side, with a one-click hold-out test on any station that has sub-daily data.
Adjustments: climate-change uplift (% or %/°C, optionally larger for short durations) and areal reduction, shown beside the baseline.
Design storms: alternating block, Chicago, SCS Type I/IA/II/III, Huff quartiles, triangular and uniform; export to CSV, SWMM (rain file and [TIMESERIES]) and HEC-HMS.
references: Koutsoyiannis, D., Kozonis, D., Manetas, A. (1998). A mathematical framework for studying rainfall intensity-duration-frequency relationships. Journal of Hydrology 206, 118–135. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-1694(98)00097-3
Hosking, J.R.M. (1990). L-moments: analysis and estimation of distributions using linear combinations of order statistics. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B 52, 105–124.
Hosking, J.R.M., Wallis, J.R. (1997). Regional Frequency Analysis: An Approach Based on L-Moments. Cambridge University Press.
Hosking, J.R.M., Wallis, J.R., Wood, E.F. (1985). Estimation of the generalized extreme-value distribution by the method of probability-weighted moments. Technometrics 27, 251–261.

Papalexiou, S.M., Dialynas, Y.G., Grimaldi, S. (2016). Hershfield factor revisited: correcting annual maximum precipitation. Journal of Hydrology 542, 884–895. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2016.09.058
Chow, V.T., Maidment, D.R., Mays, L.W. (1988). Applied Hydrology. McGraw-Hill.
Keifer, C.J., Chu, H.H. (1957). Synthetic storm pattern for drainage design. Journal of the Hydraulics Division (ASCE) 83(HY4).
Huff, F.A. (1990). Time Distributions of Heavy Rainstorms in Illinois. Illinois State Water Survey Circular 173.
USDA-NRCS (1986). Urban Hydrology for Small Watersheds, Technical Release 55; distributions as implemented in HEC-HMS 4.13.
Menabde, M., Seed, A., Pegram, G. (1999). A simple scaling model for extreme rainfall. Water Resources Research 35(1), 335–339.

Madsen, H., Rasmussen, P.F., Rosbjerg, D. (1997). Comparison of annual maximum series and partial duration series methods for modeling extreme hydrologic events. Water Resources Research 33(4), 747–757.
Efron, B., Tibshirani, R.J. (1993). An Introduction to the Bootstrap. Chapman & Hall.
brishti-idf.data: Load a rainfall record (1-minute to daily, tipping-bucket logs, or annual-maximum tables). Missing values may be blank, NA, -999 or ***; trace (T) is read as 0. All sample files are synthetic (generated by tools/make_samples.js). The only real record shipped is Denver hourly rainfall (July, 1949–1990) from the R package extRemes (GPL): see data/third-party/README.md.
validation: The numerical core is tested against SciPy (see docs/VALIDATION.md).

Generated by node tools/run_validation.js on 2026-11-03 with Node v22.23.4; reference values from SciPy 1.18.1 (tests/reference/make_reference.py) and from the published sources named per row. Result: 56 of 56 test cases passed; 363 of 363 recorded checks passed.
Methods that estimate sub-daily rainfall from daily data are not validated for Bangladesh.

Hold-out validation of daily-to-sub-daily methods: sub-daily data are hidden; only fixed calendar-day totals are used to estimate 24-h quantiles (with the 1.13 fixed-interval factor), which are then disaggregated. Denver is a single semi-arid, convective, mid-latitude station with July-only data — it is NOT representative of Bangladesh monsoon rainfall. The second dataset is synthetic. Neither establishes accuracy for Bangladesh; that needs BMD/BWDB sub-daily records.
Regional analysis (H, D, growth curve) is checked for internal identities only; it has not been cross-checked against the R package lmomRFA and is labelled EXPERIMENTAL in the tool.
The user interface is tested by a headless-browser smoke test (Chromium only).
limitations: No Bangladeshi sub-daily truth was available. Every daily-to-sub-daily result is therefore labelled experimental or "accuracy not validated".
Bell (1969) coefficients and the Leclerc–Schaake ARF formula were recalled, not checked against the original papers (labelled EXPERIMENTAL).
Stationarity is assumed. A Mann–Kendall test (no correction for serial correlation) is reported, but there is no non-stationary IDF model.
Bootstrap percentile intervals under-cover. In the tool's own tests, nominal 90% intervals covered the truth about 80% of the time for 40-year records, and the screen says so.

Peaks over threshold (v0.2) uses a known threshold equal to the smallest selected peak and Poisson arrivals. There are no bootstrap intervals for POT quantiles, and when POT is used for design the Koutsoyiannis models are not fitted.

Outlier screening is the single Grubbs–Beck test of Bulletin 17B; one outlier can mask another. The multiple Grubbs–Beck test of Bulletin 17C is not implemented. Flags are never acted on automatically.
1.13/1.04 are average factors. Papalexiou et al. (2016) show the correction is random from year to year. Where sub-daily data exist, use the empirical factor the tool reports.
Climate uplift is a simple multiplier (% or %/°C). It does not downscale GCMs. No Bangladesh-specific areal reduction factors are built in.

dependability.pageTitle: Dependability Analyzer — dependable water level, flow & rainfall · Mahfujur Rahman Joy
dependability.problem: Dependable water levels, flows and rainfall from long records. Filter years and months, convert the datum, rank with a plotting position, and take report-ready figures and tables into your report.
method: Each ranked value gets a plotting position. Weibull (the default, as in the report workbook) is D = R × 100 / (n + 1); Gringorten, Cunnane and Hazen use D = (R − a) × 100 / (n + 1 − 2a) with a = 0.44, 0.4 and 0.5. Low side is ranked high to low, high side low to high.
The value at P is taken at rank ROUND(P/100 × (n + 1 − 2a) + a), which for Weibull is the report's ROUND(P/100 × (n+1)), or interpolated between ranks if you choose that.
With one value per year, "dependable value in the year" uses the same rule inside each year, then the years are ranked.
Low side: value equalled or exceeded P % of the time (dependable flow, dependable low level). High side: value not exceeded P % of the time (dependable high level).
dependability.data: Excel (.xlsx) or CSV: daily, monthly or yearly values with a date column, Year and Month columns, or a Year × Jan…Dec table. BWDB files repeat readings as HIGH / LOW rows; keep only the regular ones. 'Try an example series' loads a made-up example series, not real measurements.

cn-calculator.pageTitle: Composite CN Calculator — SCS curve number and runoff · Mahfujur Rahman Joy
cn-calculator.problem: Area-weighted SCS curve number (TR-55 / NEH-4) for every sub-catchment: paste a land-use table from Excel, get CN for AMC I, II and III, retention, initial abstraction, design-storm runoff and volume. Runs in your browser; files are never uploaded.
method: CN(II) = Σ(Aᵢ·CNᵢ) / ΣAᵢ (CNᵢ for the sub-catchment's soil group)
S = 25400/CN − 254 (mm); Ia = λ·S (NEH-4 uses 0.20)
Q = (P − Ia)² / (P − Ia + S) for P > Ia, else 0; C = Q/P
V = Q·A·10 m³ (A in ha); with water excluded, A is the land area only
Soil textures map to hydrologic soil groups, open water can count at CN 100 or be left out, and the CN lookup for Bangladesh land-cover classes is editable.
cn-calculator.data: Click a cell, then paste (Ctrl+V) a block copied from Excel. If your block starts with a header row, columns are matched by name in any order. Areas in hectares. Soil accepts a texture (e.g. Clay Loam) or a group letter A–D. CN lookup: values from your workbook's CN_Lookup sheet (TR-55 analogues). The sheet opens with 'Rows 1–3: sample from your workbook'.

samples.label: Built-in sample rows ('Rows 1–3: sample from your workbook': Catchment 1–3), shown on first load and restored by the 'Reset to workbook defaults' button

river-profile.pageTitle: River Profile Studio — Cross-sections, SOBEK Y-Z & profiling · Mahfujur Rahman Joy
river-profile.problem: Convert surveyed river cross-sections into SOBEK CRDS ... lt yz definitions. Check and edit points visually, orient left bank first, add vertical walls, and export a clean PROFILE.DEF. Runs 100% in your browser.
method: Cross-Section Inspector (Y-Z): interactively inspect and edit elevations and distances, add or delete specific survey points, select custom left and right bank codes for orientation.
Datum shift to Z (m): MSL → PWD in Bangladesh is typically +0.46 m. Section names in SOBEK become Prefix + ID.
Vertical wall at beginning & end: None (SOBEK standard extension); Add wall of size / height (+H m); Wall to fixed level (Z = … m).
Bank crest trimming (optional — off by default): keeps only the main channel between the natural bank crests.
Output: without a file, a clean new PROFILE.DEF is written. With an existing file, matching section names are updated in place.

Thalweg & Longitudinal Profiler (L-Profile): automatically tracks the lowest bed points to plot longitudinal thalweg profiles and 2D alignment maps. Shows Thalweg Bed Profile, Left Bank Crest, Right Bank Crest, Mean Bed Gradient (S₀) and an optional Water Surface; Reach Stations Checklist & Local Gradients; Export Thalweg CSV and Export 3D GeoJSON.
river-profile.data: Drop an Excel or CSV file (.xlsx · .xls · .csv · .txt) with Cross-section ID, Distance Y (m), Level Z (m) and an optional bank / data code; optional Easting / Longitude (X), Northing / Latitude (Y) and River / Reach / Khal name for the thalweg profile and map. 'Load sample survey' loads a built-in sample (9 sections in 2 reaches).
limitations: Produces SOBEK 2.1x CRDS … ty 10 … lt yz blocks. Verify in SOBEK Data Edit before model execution.

ababahika.pageTitle: Ababahika — catchment slope, land cover & soil statistics · Mahfujur Rahman Joy
ababahika.problem: Slope, land-cover and soil-texture statistics for every catchment, with a map and basic geoprocessing. Runs entirely in the browser; files are never uploaded.
method: Cell-in-polygon: cell centre inside (GDAL rasterize scanline rule; same as rasterio/rasterstats all_touched=False and ArcGIS Zonal Statistics). Holes and multipart polygons handled.
Polygons are reprojected to the raster CRS (proj4js); rasters are never resampled for statistics.
Slope: Horn (1981), NoData neighbours replaced by the centre value (ArcGIS rule), edges replicated. Geographic DEMs: per-row metre spacing from WGS 84 radii of curvature.
Areas: projected cells |Δx·Δy|; geographic cells exact ellipsoidal area; catchment areas geodesic (WGS 84, local Lambert equal-area); polygon-on-polygon (soil) areas in the catchment's UTM zone.

Hydrology (D8): DEM at its own or a coarser cell size; embankments burned in as walls (4-connected), sluices/regulators as openings and outlets, khals burned in as channels (shapefile or drawn on the map); Priority-Flood filling (Barnes et al. 2014, +ε for flats); D8 flow direction (ESRI codes 1–128); flow accumulation; stream network with Strahler order; drainage units per sluice, or per clicked/loaded pour point snapped to the largest flow.

Tools (GDAL 3 in WebAssembly): project raster, clip raster (polygons or map view), merge/mosaic rasters, slope raster, clip vector, merge vectors, dissolve, export vector (shapefile, GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KML, CSV) in any coordinate system.
references: Horn, B.K.P. (1981). Hill shading and the reflectance map. Proceedings of the IEEE, 69(1), 14–47.
Strahler, A.N. (1952). Hypsometric (area-altitude) analysis of erosional topography. GSA Bulletin, 63, 1117–1142.
ababahika.data: Drop files on the map or press ＋ Add data. Shapefiles: a .zip, or select the .shp, .dbf and .prj together. Rasters: GeoTIFF of any size (read in pieces, never loaded whole); .img, .asc and others are converted with GDAL. Demo data: 'Demo: catchment statistics' and 'Demo: polder drainage units' (tools/ababahika/data/demo/).
validation: Reference implementations: rasterio 1.4 (geometry_mask, all_touched=False), NumPy Horn slope, shapely 2 intersections, pyproj Geod areas. Synthetic data from tests/make_data.py (seeded).
tests/zonal.test.mjs: 183/183 checks — identical cell counts, slope statistics to 1e-9°, class areas to 1e-6 m², soil overlay areas to 0.02 %, geodesic areas to 0.01 %.

tests/hydro.test.mjs (tests/make_hydro.py): 22/22 — exact fill identical to pysheds fill_depressions (3 926 raised cells); D8 identical to an independent NumPy D8 on every interior cell (pysheds 0.5 flowdir is unreliable under NumPy 2); flow accumulation identical to pysheds accumulation from the same directions; catchments identical to pysheds catchment.
tests/slope.test.mjs: slope rasters vs NumPy Horn, max difference 1e-6° (float32), identical NoData mask and georeferencing.
Demo polder (2 sluices): units 21.78 + 21.64 km² vs polder polygon 43.38 km².
Not yet validated: real Bangladeshi DEMs (SRTM/ALOS/FABDEM) against ArcGIS Pro outputs — recommended before first use in a report.
limitations: D8 on a DEM alone is unreliable in floodplains and polders. Burn in embankments, sluices and khals, prefer a bare-earth DEM (survey/LiDAR, FABDEM), and read each unit's Flat % (cells with no lower neighbour) and Filled % (cells raised by depression filling): where they are high, the boundary was set by the filling algorithm, not the terrain.
GDAL tools copy inputs into memory: inputs + outputs must fit in roughly 2 GB.
Slope raster: up to 250 million cells (uncompressed output).
Hydrology holds the whole grid in memory: up to 40 million cells (e.g. 6 300 × 6 300; 190 km square at 30 m). Use a coarser cell size or clip the DEM for larger areas.
Not yet validated: real Bangladeshi DEMs (SRTM/ALOS/FABDEM) against ArcGIS Pro outputs — recommended before first use in a report.

hydro-ml.pageTitle: Hydro ML Studio — machine learning for water level, discharge & rainfall · Mahfujur Rahman Joy
hydro-ml.problem: Train and compare machine-learning models to simulate or forecast water level, discharge or rainfall. Lag features, eight models (SVR, random forest, gradient boosting, neural network and more), cross-validation, automatic tuning and hydrology metrics.
method: Simulate: inputs at the same time step are known, e.g. rebuilding a missing record from rainfall on the same day. Forecast: only data at least h steps old may be used, so the model predicts the target h steps ahead — the honest setting for early warning.

Lag analysis: for an input, cross-correlation with the target at each lag — peaks show the travel time. For the target itself: partial autocorrelation (PACF), the extra information each past value adds once the shorter lags are known. Computed on the training period only.

Splitting the record: the model learns from the training part and is judged on the test part it never saw. Keep the split chronological for time series: random rows let the model peek at the day before and after, which makes scores look better than they really are.

Which models? Start with the baselines (persistence, climatology): a useful model must beat them. Tree ensembles (random forest, extra trees, gradient boosting) and SVR are usually the strongest on hydrological data; linear regression is the easiest to explain. Train several and compare.

Cross-validation: repeats training and testing on different slices of the training period to see how stable a model is. Time-series: each fold trains on the past and tests on the next block (no peeking ahead). Blocked k-fold: the record is cut into k blocks and each block is tested once.

Search methods: Grid search tries every combination of the listed values — thorough but slow. Random search samples combinations at random — often as good with far fewer trials. Bayesian optimisation fits a Gaussian-process model of score vs settings and picks the next trial where improvement is most likely (expected improvement) — usually the fewest trials.

Performance was evaluated with the Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE; Nash and Sutcliffe, 1970), the Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE; Gupta et al., 2009), the coefficient of determination (R²), RMSE, MAE, percent bias (PBIAS) and the RMSE–observations standard deviation ratio (RSR).

Importance methods: Built-in comes from the model itself (how much the trees’ splits on a feature reduce error, or standardized coefficients for linear models). Permutation shuffles one feature at a time on the test period and measures the drop in NSE — slower, but works for every model and is easier to compare.
references: Gupta, H. V., Kling, H., Yilmaz, K. K., & Martinez, G. F. (2009). Decomposition of the mean squared error and NSE performance criteria. Journal of Hydrology, 377(1–2), 80–91.
Moriasi, D. N., et al. (2007). Model evaluation guidelines for systematic quantification of accuracy in watershed simulations. Transactions of the ASABE, 50(3), 885–900.
Nash, J. E., & Sutcliffe, J. V. (1970). River flow forecasting through conceptual models part I. Journal of Hydrology, 10(3), 282–290.
Joy, M. R. (2026). Hydro ML Studio [Software]. https://meawman.github.io/tools/hydro-ml/
hydro-ml.data: An .xlsx, .csv or .txt file with a date column and one or more numeric columns — for example daily rainfall, upstream water level and the downstream water level you want to predict. Dates and numbers are detected automatically. BWDB downloads list each day several times: REGULAR readings plus HIGH and LOW tide / peak readings; keeping only REGULAR rows gives one consistent reading per time step. 'Try an example' loads a built-in example marked 'EXAMPLE · SYNTHETIC DATA'.
limitations: Ratings combine NSE, RSR and PBIAS thresholds of Moriasi et al. (2007), written for monthly streamflow — use them as a guide for other variables and time steps.
Linear regression: cannot capture thresholds or non-linear runoff on its own.
K-nearest neighbours: simple and assumption-free, but cannot predict beyond the range it has seen (e.g. a record flood) and slows down on long records.
Neural network (multi-layer perceptron): flexible and smooth but needs more data and is more sensitive to settings.
Models that use past target values fill gaps recursively: each predicted step feeds the next one.

dsbc.pageTitle: DSBC Studio — downscaling and bias correction · Mahfujur Rahman Joy
dsbc.problem: Calibrate on the past, correct the future. Statistical downscaling and bias correction for daily, weekly or monthly climate series, with honest validation. Everything runs in this browser tab; your files are never uploaded.
method: Screen predictors with partial informational correlation, train and honestly validate 11 regression models, then correct climate-model runs with 10 univariate and 5 multivariate methods, checking that each correction keeps the model's projected change.

Partial informational correlation (PIC): how much new information a candidate adds about the local variable once the already selected predictors are known. It is based on mutual information, so curved and threshold relationships count too, and redundant predictors (mean, maximum and minimum temperature together) score low. Sharma & Mehrotra (2014).

Validation scheme: Blocked K-fold cuts the record into K blocks of whole years; each block is predicted by a model trained on the others. Hold-out trains on the first part and tests on the last. Expanding window always trains on the past and tests the next block, like a forecast.

Hyperparameter tuning: settings such as the number of neighbours or the depth of trees are chosen inside each training fold, with a time-ordered 3-fold cross-validation of the training data only, so test data never influence them.

Every bias correction is calibrated on the overlap of observations and the historical run and applied with those fixed parameters to the future. Standardising a future series with its own mean and spread removes the projected change entirely.

Daily, weekly and monthly data are handled at their own time step and can be aggregated to a coarser one in each step (rainfall-like variables are summed, others averaged). Nested methods correct the data's own step first and then the coarser ones (for daily data: day, month, year); for daily rainfall the daily level only rescales amounts, so dry days stay dry.

Downscaling skill is judged on years the model has not seen and against a forecast that repeats the average seasonal cycle (calendar-month means, or a smoothed day-of-year cycle for daily data), because the seasonal cycle alone gives high R² for most hydro-climatic variables.
Python methods run locally through Pyodide; source code and Jupyter workflow in the accompanying dsbc package.
references: Linear scaling: Lenderink et al. (2007); Teutschbein & Seibert (2012)
Empirical quantile mapping (EQM): Panofsky & Brier (1968); Gudmundsson et al. (2012)
Quantile delta mapping (QDM): Cannon et al. (2015); port of R package MBC
Scaled distribution mapping (SDM): Switanek et al. (2017)
CDF-transform (CDF-t): Michelangeli et al. (2009)
Nested bias correction (NBC): Johnson & Sharma (2012)
MRNBC (multivariate recursive nested): Mehrotra & Sharma (2015, 2016)
MBCp (Pearson), MBCr (Spearman): Cannon (2016)
MBCn (N-pdf transform): Cannon (2018)
R2D2 (rank resampling): Vrac (2018)
PIC-weighted k-NN (NPRED): Sharma & Mehrotra (2014); Sharma et al. (2016)
Multiple linear regression: SDSM-type regression (Wilby et al., 2002)
dsbc.data: Use CSV or Excel files with a date column and one column per variable, at a daily, weekly or monthly time step. Each Excel sheet is read as one station. Demo data: the demo is set up like a real study, with invented daily data: rain-gauge and thermometer records at two stations (1991 to 2020), ERA5-style large-scale predictors over each station, and a CMIP6-style historical and SSP5-8.5 run.
validation: Each method was implemented from its original paper or translated from the authors' code, and checked against independent reference implementations.
Linear and variance scaling: identical to python-cmethods 2.3 (maximum difference 0.0000).
Scaled distribution mapping, CDF-t: identical to ibicus 1.3 with running windows switched off (maximum difference 0.0000).

Empirical quantile mapping, QDM: agree with xsdba (xclim) at r = 0.9997; differences come from where quantile nodes are placed. QDM, MBCp, MBCr, MBCn and R2D2 are translations of A. J. Cannon's R package MBC 0.10-8.

MRNBC: independent implementation from Mehrotra and Sharma (2015, 2016, 2021). On the UNSW MBC package's monthly rainfall example (15 sites, 70 years) the corrected series correlate with the UNSW output at r = 0.98 (calibration) and 0.91 (validation), with similar errors in means, spreads, lag-1 and cross-correlations.
PIC: implemented from Sharma and Mehrotra (2014); on synthetic data it selects the true non-linear drivers and rejects redundant and irrelevant candidates.
limitations: Climate-model data on a 360-day calendar must be converted to real dates first; no-leap calendars work as they are.

With long daily records, settings are tuned on at most 3,000 evenly spaced values, SVR, Gaussian processes and PIC-kNN are fitted on a thinned sample, and each tree of a forest sees 3,000 values, so the browser stays responsive.
PIC: long daily records are estimated on a random sample of 800 time steps.

Nested bias correction rescales year-to-year variability, which also rescales trends. The default here removes the model's smooth 21-year climate signal before correcting and puts it back afterwards; the original behaviour is available for comparison.
The first visit downloads about 40 MB; the browser caches it for later visits. Pyodide loads from cdn.jsdelivr.net.
Demo data are invented with random numbers, but laid out like a real study.
